sections.title: Reflection using preparation and its inverse

opening: Deutsch’s algorithm answered a question about a function with a single interference step. Many tasks instead ask for a particular input: an item that passes a test we can check but cannot invert. Classically, finding one marked item among \(N\) requires checking a number of candidates proportional to \(N\). Can interference concentrate probability on the marked item faster?
opening_continuation: We start with four items, where every amplitude can be followed by hand: a phase oracle marks the answer with a sign, and a reflection about the mean turns the sign into certainty. For larger searches we group the marked and unmarked items, which reduces the whole evolution to a rotation in a plane. The rotation explains both the speedup, about \(\sqrt N\) iterations instead of \(N\) queries, and its danger: rotating too far undoes the gain, so knowing when to stop is part of the algorithm. Finally we extend the method from a uniform start to any preparation and any test of success.
So far, oracles and reflections have been treated as single operations. The next chapter asks how such operations are built from elementary gates.
